title: The Missing Check
blurb: The hardest flaws to see are the ones that aren't there — a control that SHOULD exist but doesn't. Read code that looks fine and name what's absent.

levels.title: L1 · The admin action
levels.prompt: Any signed-in user can reach this. What's the security problem?
levels.hint: [Authorize] answers "are you logged in?" — does anything here check WHO you are or WHAT you're allowed to do?

blocks.label: Code

options.label: Missing an authorization check — any logged-in user can call it

levels.explain: [Authorize] only confirms the caller is authenticated (logged in) — it does NOT limit WHICH users. A regular user could POST to admin/delete-all and wipe the table. It needs a role/policy check, e.g. [Authorize(Roles = "Admin")] or a policy. Authentication ≠ authorization.

failStates.title: Authentication is present
failStates.explain: [Authorize] already requires the user to be logged in. What's missing is authorization — restricting this destructive action to admins.

failStates.title: It's wide open to any user
failStates.explain: A destructive admin action reachable by every authenticated user is a serious broken-access-control flaw. It needs a role or policy check.

levels.title: L2 · The file upload
levels.prompt: It saves an uploaded file. What's missing?
levels.hint: Think about WHAT gets uploaded and WHERE it lands. Is the type or size checked? Is the folder served to the web?

blocks.label: Code

options.label: No type/size check, and it saves into a web-served folder under the user's own filename

levels.explain: Three missing controls compound: the file type/size is never validated, the attacker chooses the filename (path traversal again), and it's written into _webroot — a folder the server hands back over HTTP. An attacker uploads shell.aspx and then requests it, running code on your server. Validate type/size, generate your own filename, and store outside the web root.

failStates.title: Encryption isn't the gap
failStates.explain: The problem isn't confidentiality of the file — it's that an unvalidated, attacker-named file lands in a web-executable folder.

failStates.title: This is a classic RCE path
failStates.explain: Unrestricted upload into the web root is a well-known route to remote code execution. The missing type/size validation and the attacker-controlled path/location are the flaw.

levels.title: L3 · The password reset
levels.prompt: This resets a password. What's missing?
levels.hint: What proves the person asking actually owns that email account?

blocks.label: Code

options.label: No proof of ownership — anyone can reset anyone's password by email, with no verification token

levels.explain: Nothing verifies that the caller actually controls that email address. An attacker just POSTs someone else's email + a new password and takes over the account. A reset must require a secret, single-use, expiring token that was emailed to the account owner (ASP.NET Core Identity generates one). The hashing here is fine — the missing ownership check is the hole.

failStates.title: The password IS hashed
failStates.explain: It uses _hasher.HashPassword (Identity's PBKDF2 hasher — a slow, salted password hash). Hashing isn't the problem; the missing verification token is.

failStates.title: It's a full account-takeover
failStates.explain: With no token proving ownership, anyone can reset any account's password just by knowing the email. That's account takeover.
